Authors: Simon Priest, Stephen D. Ritchie

Source: Springer eBooks

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution; Canada-related term in title: canadian; Canada-related term in abstract: canada

Abstract: Abstract This chapter examines trends and transformations in outdoor health in Canada. After defining outdoor health, summarizing the health benefits of nature, and explaining the transdisciplinary character of outdoor health, Canada and its healthcare system are introduced. Several trends that are transforming outdoor health in Canada are then examined in more detail: land-based healing, nature prescription, outdoor learning, wild pedagogies, risky outdoor play, outdoor therapies, and ecohealth promotion. Since more than one of these resources has Indigenous content, an explanation of Canada’s history and politics surrounding Indigeneity is provided. The chapter concludes with a discussion of wellness practices, summarizing the transformational trend elements that impact outdoor health and benefit the six dimensions of well-being, as outlined in the Holistic Model of Health Promotion.

Authors: Stephen Reysen, Courtney N. Plante, Sharon E. Roberts, Kathleen Carrese Gerbasi

Source: Emerald Group Publishing Limited eBooks

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Prior research shows that fanship – the extent to which a person identifies with the object of their fandom – is a robust predictor of fan collecting behavior (Reysen et al., 2021; Reysen & Plante, 2023). To date, however, there has been little research investigating the possible mechanisms driving this association, including bonding and forming bridges with other fans, fan capital, fans’ fear of missing out, tendency to hoard, and a felt need to belong. A mediation analysis (controlling for participant age and gender) showed that a significant association between fanship and collecting was mediated by all six proposed mechanisms, with fear of missing out being the only negative pathway. These results shed light on the potentially dual-edged nature of fan collection as both functional (e.g., a source of social capital) and maladaptive (e.g., hoarding).
